Figure 15: ArUco marker placement The OpenCV marker detection code provides the image coordinate of the detected marker’s center. Since we also know the depth value at that image coordinate (because the depth map and the image are aligned) we can compute the marker center’s 3D Page 16 of 31 spherical coordinates (rho, theta, phi), which can then be converted to 3D Cartesian coordinates (X, Y, Z) in the arm’s frame of reference. Determining the rho component of the spherical coordinates is the most complex part, requiring de-projecting the depth measurement at the marker center’s pixel coordinate. This is needed because the lidar’s depth measurement represents distance along a normal from the image plane to the scene location, whereas rho is the Euclidian distance from the camera center to the scene location. To account for the camera lens distortion, the de-projection needs to take the camera’s intrinsic calibration into account. The conversion from spherical to Cartesian is straightforward, but the resulting X,Y,Z is in the camera’s reference frame. Transforming to the ARM base reference frame requires careful calibration of the camera’s extrinsics with respect to the ARM base. The principle behind determining the yaw of a surface with respect to the camera plane is based on trigonometry. Knowing two points on the same horizontal line on the fuel cell’s front surface, the angle between the vector connecting those two points and the camera plane can be derived directly from the trigonometric definition of the cosine. One point is the center of the left marker, which was used for estimating the 3D pose. Using the exact same technique for the right marker provides the second point. Demonstration (without Hydrogen) The autonomous dispenser prototype accomplished a huge technical milestone by successfully completing 199 out of 200 connection attempts, although these connections were done without hydrogen. For this test, the fuel cell was placed on a pallet moved by an AGV. The AGV was programmed to move near the robot and stop. The robot then aligned the nozzle with the receptacle, mated the two and lock the nozzle to the receptacle. Once completed, the robot would then disconnect the nozzle and return to its home position. The AGV would then move the fuel cell away from the dispenser and then return for the next attempt. Figure 16: Screen capture from video of 199 successful trials.
